module_title: Sustainable and Green Supply Chain Management

lessons.title: Triple Bottom Line and Sustainability
lessons.body: The Triple Bottom Line (TBL) is a way to measure business success beyond just profit. It looks at three Ps: Profit, People, and Planet. In African supply chains, this means you consider financial gain, social impact (like fair wages and community well-being), and environmental impact (like waste and pollution). For example, a Kenyan coffee exporter using TBL might track profit per kilogram, number of farmers paid a living wage, and water usage per sack. A simple tool is a scorecard: list 3-5 metrics for each P. Profit: revenue, cost, profit margin. People: number of local jobs, safety incidents, training hours. Planet: carbon emissions, water use, waste sent to landfill. You can use Excel or free tools like the B Impact Assessment to get started. In Africa, TBL helps businesses attract impact investors and meet buyer demands. For instance, a Ghanaian shea butter supplier increased sales to European cosmetics firms by documenting fair trade practices and reduced deforestation. To apply TBL, start by mapping your supply chain activities. Identify where you create negative social or environmental impacts. Then set targets: e.g., reduce water use by 20% in one year, or ensure all suppliers pay at least minimum wage. Report progress annually. Remember, TBL is not just about being nice; it builds resilience. Climate change, resource scarcity, and social unrest directly affect your supply chain. By balancing the three Ps, you reduce risks and open new markets. For small businesses, begin with one metric per P. For example, a Nigerian tomato farmer might track profit per crate, number of workers with health insurance, and kilograms of compost produced from waste. Over time, expand. The key is to measure, act, and communicate. African consumers and governments increasingly favour sustainable businesses, so TBL can be a competitive advantage.

lessons.title: Green Procurement and Supplier Environmental Compliance
lessons.body: Green procurement means buying goods and services that have the least environmental impact. For African businesses, this starts with your suppliers. You need to know if they comply with environmental laws and if they are reducing their footprint. First, set clear criteria. For example, require suppliers to have an environmental policy, to measure their carbon emissions, and to avoid hazardous chemicals. Use a supplier questionnaire. Ask about waste disposal, energy sources, and water management. In South Africa, companies often ask for ISO 14001 certification, which is an international standard for environmental management. But many small African suppliers cannot afford certification. So you can offer training or a phased approach. For instance, a Zambian textile company worked with local cotton farmers to reduce pesticide use by switching to organic methods. They provided training and a price premium. To verify compliance, conduct audits. A simple audit checklist includes: Does the supplier have a permit for waste discharge? Are chemicals stored safely? Is there evidence of energy efficiency? You can also use third-party tools like Sedex or EcoVadis, which rate supplier sustainability. In Africa, mobile apps like Ulula allow workers to report issues anonymously. When you find non-compliance, don't just drop the supplier. Work with them on a corrective action plan with deadlines. For example, a Kenyan flower farm found that a supplier was dumping pesticides into a river. They helped build a proper disposal site and trained staff. Now, the supplier is compliant and the farm avoids reputational damage. Green procurement also means buying locally to reduce transport emissions. A Nigerian food processor sources cassava from nearby farms instead of importing starch from Asia, cutting carbon footprint by 30%. To start, review your top 10 suppliers. Ask them to complete a self-assessment. Then prioritize those with the biggest impact. Set annual improvement targets. Communicate your expectations in contracts. And celebrate successes. By greening procurement, you reduce risk, save money through efficiency, and protect your brand.

lessons.title: Reverse Logistics and Circular Economy
lessons.body: Reverse logistics is the process of moving goods from the customer back to the producer. It includes returns, repairs, recycling, and disposal. In a circular economy, you design products and processes to keep materials in use as long as possible. For African supply chains, this can turn waste into profit. Take e-waste. Africa generates over 3 million tonnes of e-waste annually, but only 10-20% is formally recycled. A company in Ghana, like AGbogbloshie's informal recyclers, recovers copper and gold. You can set up a take-back scheme. For example, a Kenyan mobile phone retailer offers a discount when customers return old phones. The phones are refurbished and resold, or dismantled for parts. This reduces landfill and creates jobs. Another example: a South African beverage company collects empty bottles and reuses them. They set up collection points at schools and shops, paying 50 cents per bottle. The bottles are washed and refilled, cutting glass production by 40%. To implement reverse logistics, start with a product that has high return value. Map the flow: where do products end up? How can you get them back? Use simple tools: a reverse logistics cost calculator in Excel. Consider transport: backhauling â using trucks that would otherwise return empty â reduces cost and emissions. For instance, a Zambian dairy delivers milk to stores and picks up empty crates on the return trip. For circular economy, think about design. Can you make products modular so parts can be replaced? Can you use biodegradable packaging? A Rwandan coffee exporter switched to jute bags that customers return for a deposit. The bags are reused five times. To measure success, track recovery rate, cost savings, and waste diverted. Start small: pilot a take-back program for one product. Partner with local recyclers or waste pickers. In Africa, informal waste collectors are key. Integrate them into your system, pay them fairly, and provide safety gear. Reverse logistics and circular economy not only reduce environmental harm but also build customer loyalty and reduce raw material costs.

lessons.title: Carbon Footprint Measurement in Supply Chains
lessons.body: A carbon footprint is the total greenhouse gases (GHG) emitted by your activities, measured in carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e). For a supply chain, you need to measure emissions from sourcing, production, transport, storage, and disposal. In Africa, transport and agriculture are major sources. To start, use the GHG Protocol, a global standard. It divides emissions into three scopes: Scope 1 (direct emissions from your own vehicles, generators), Scope 2 (indirect from purchased electricity), and Scope 3 (all other indirect emissions from suppliers, customers, etc.). Most African businesses focus on Scope 1 and 2 first. For example, a Nigerian manufacturer can measure diesel used in generators (Scope 1) and electricity from the grid (Scope 2). To calculate, use emission factors. The IPCC provides factors: diesel emits 2.68 kg CO2e per litre; grid electricity in South Africa is about 0.95 kg CO2e per kWh. Multiply activity data by the factor. For a small truck doing 100 km per day at 10 litres/100km, that's 10 litres * 2.68 = 26.8 kg CO2e per day. For Scope 3, you need supplier data. Send a questionnaire asking for their energy use and transport. Tools like the GHG Protocol's Scope 3 Evaluator can help. In Africa, mobile apps like CarbonTrack or free spreadsheets from the CDP can simplify. Once you have a baseline, set reduction targets. For example, a Kenyan flower farm switched from air freight to sea freight for some shipments, cutting transport emissions by 90% per kilogram. A Ghanaian cocoa cooperative trained farmers to use less fertilizer, reducing nitrous oxide emissions. To reduce your footprint, consider: energy efficiency (solar panels, LED lights), logistics optimization (consolidate shipments, use rail instead of trucks), and supplier engagement. Measure progress annually. Report to stakeholders. Many international buyers now require carbon footprint data. For instance, European retailers ask African suppliers for their carbon footprint as part of sustainability scorecards. By measuring and reducing, you can win contracts and save costs. Start simple: track fuel and electricity bills. Use free online calculators. Then expand to suppliers. Remember, what gets measured gets managed.

lessons.title: Regulations and Standards for Sustainability
lessons.body: Sustainability regulations and standards are rules that governments and international bodies set to protect the environment and society. For African supply chains, knowing these is crucial to avoid fines, lost contracts, and reputational damage. Key international standards include ISO 14001 (environmental management), ISO 26000 (social responsibility), and SA8000 (fair labour). In Africa, many countries have national environmental laws. For example, Kenya's Environmental Management and Co-ordination Act (EMCA) requires businesses to conduct Environmental Impact Assessments (EIA) and obtain licenses. Nigeria has the National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency (NESREA) that enforces laws on waste, water, and air quality. South Africa's National Environmental Management Act (NEMA) sets strict rules on pollution. If you export to Europe or America, you must meet their regulations. The EU's Green Deal and its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) will tax imports based on carbon footprint, starting with cement, steel, and fertilizers. This affects African exporters. For instance, a South African steel maker must report emissions to EU importers or face tariffs. Similarly, the US Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act bans imports from certain regions, so you must prove no forced labour. To comply, first identify which regulations apply to you. Check your country's environmental agency website. For exports, ask your buyer what standards they require. Common ones: GlobalG.A.P. for agriculture, Fairtrade for cocoa and coffee, and FSC for timber. Certification can be costly, but there are group certifications for smallholders. For example, a cooperative of 500 cocoa farmers in CÃ´te d'Ivoire got Fairtrade certified together, sharing the cost. To prepare for audits, keep records: waste disposal receipts, training logs, wage records. Use free templates from the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI). Also, train staff on compliance. A Zambian mining supplier avoided a shutdown by training workers on spill prevention. Finally, stay updated. Regulations change. Join industry associations like the African Circular Economy Alliance. By understanding and following regulations, you protect your business and contribute to sustainable development.

lessons.title: Case Study: Patagonia's Sustainable Supply Chain
lessons.body: Patagonia is an American outdoor clothing company known for its strong commitment to sustainability. Its supply chain offers lessons for African businesses. Patagonia's mission is to 'build the best product, cause no unnecessary harm, and use business to inspire and implement solutions to the environmental crisis.' They apply the Triple Bottom Line throughout. In procurement, Patagonia uses the Higg Index, a tool to measure environmental and social impacts of materials. They require suppliers to meet strict standards, including fair labour and chemical safety. They audit factories regularly and publish a list of suppliers. For example, they work with a factory in Kenya? Actually, Patagonia sources from factories in Vietnam, China, and other parts of Asia, but the principles apply to Africa. They use recycled materials: 87% of their line uses recycled fabrics. They offer a repair service, Worn Wear, which fixes broken items instead of throwing them away. They also have a take-back program for old clothes, which are recycled into new fibers. This is reverse logistics and circular economy in action. Patagonia measures its carbon footprint across Scopes 1, 2, and 3. They aim to be carbon neutral by 2025. They invest in renewable energy in their supply chain. For African businesses, key takeaways: 1) Set a clear sustainability mission. 2) Use tools like the Higg Index or free self-assessment. 3) Collaborate with suppliers to improve, not just punish. 4) Innovate in circularity: repair, reuse, recycle. 5) Be transparent: publish your progress. Patagonia's supply chain is not perfect, but their approach shows that sustainability can drive brand loyalty and profitability. For example, their Worn Wear program increased customer engagement and reduced waste. A Kenyan clothing brand could start a repair service for school uniforms. A Ghanaian textile recycler could partner with brands to take back old clothes. Patagonia also supports grassroots environmental activism, donating 1% of sales. African businesses can support local conservation. To apply: start with a material assessment. Identify your most used fabric or material. Find a recycled or sustainable alternative. Then set up a take-back scheme. Train staff on repair. Communicate your story. Patagonia proves that sustainability is a journey, not a destination.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Sustainable and Green Supply Chain Management in African Agribusiness

Sustainability is no longer a compliance burden for African agribusinessesâit is a market access strategy. European retailers, development finance institutions, and African governments increasingly require verifiable environmental and social performance across supply chains. This practical reference distils the operational essentials of sustainable and green supply chain management for African agribusiness managers, covering the triple bottom line, green procurement, reverse logistics, carbon measurement, and the regulatory landscape. It closes with a case study of Patagonia and a ready-to-use checklist.

1. The Triple Bottom Line: Profit, People, Planet

The triple bottom line (TBL) framework, coined by John Elkington in 1994, requires businesses to measure performance across three dimensions: economic profit, social equity (people), and environmental integrity (planet). For African agribusinesses, the TBL is not abstract. A cocoa cooperative in Ghana that pays below-living wages will face supplier delisting under EU due diligence rules. A Kenyan flower farm that over-irrigates will lose its certification and its European supermarket contract. A Zambian soybean processor that ignores soil health will see yields collapse within a decade.

Operationally, TBL translates into three sets of metrics: financial (gross margin, cost per tonne, return on assets), social (living wage gap, child labour incidence, gender inclusion, worker safety), and environmental (water use per kg, GHG emissions per tonne, waste diversion rate, soil organic carbon). These metrics must be tracked at the same frequency as financial accountsâmonthly or quarterlyânot annually.

2. Green Procurement and Supplier Environmental Compliance

Green procurement embeds environmental criteria into purchasing decisions. For African agribusinesses buying from smallholder farmers or aggregators, this means supplier codes of conduct, environmental screening questionnaires, and audit rights. Practical criteria include: no deforestation on supplier farms after a cut-off date (e.g., 2020), integrated pest management instead of banned pesticides, water abstraction permits, and traceability to farm level.

Supplier compliance should be tiered: self-assessment for low-risk suppliers, desk review for medium-risk, and on-site audit for high-risk (e.g., those near protected areas or with prior violations). Non-compliance triggers a corrective action plan with clear deadlines, not immediate delistingâthis protects smallholder livelihoods while driving improvement.

Procurement Criterion Verification Method Typical African Risk
No deforestation post-2020 Satellite imagery + farm geolocation Cocoa expansion into Ghanaian forest reserves
Banned pesticide exclusion Residue testing + purchase receipts Use of paraquat in Kenyan horticulture
Water abstraction compliance Permit review + metered abstraction Over-abstraction from Lake Naivasha catchment
Living wage / income Payroll audit + farm income survey Cocoa farm-gate prices below living income
Traceability to farm Polygon mapping + chain of custody Mixing of certified and non-certified beans

Source: Compiled from Rainforest Alliance (2020) Sustainable Agriculture Standard and ISEAL Alliance guidance on supply chain traceability.

3. Reverse Logistics and the Circular Economy

Reverse logistics is the flow of goods from the point of consumption back to the point of origin for reuse, recycling, or disposal. In African agribusiness, reverse logistics applies to packaging (jute bags, plastic crates, pesticide containers), organic waste (coffee husk, cocoa pod husk, rice straw), and by-products (molasses, oil palm kernel cake). The circular economy principle is simple: waste from one process becomes input to another.

Examples: coffee husk in Ethiopia is briquetted for fuel or composted; cocoa pod husk in Ghana is processed into animal feed and potash; plastic pesticide containers are collected and recycled under container management schemes. These are not charityâthey reduce input costs, generate new revenue, and cut disposal liabilities.

Waste Stream Circular Use African Example Business Benefit
Coffee husk Briquettes, compost, mushroom substrate Ethiopia, Uganda Fuel cost reduction, soil fertility
Cocoa pod husk Animal feed, potash, biochar Ghana, CÃ´te d'Ivoire Feed savings, fertilizer substitution
Pesticide containers Triple-rinse + recycling Kenya (CropLife scheme) Compliance, brand protection
Rice straw Fodder, bioenergy, packaging Nigeria, Tanzania Reduced burning, new revenue
Palm kernel cake Animal feed Nigeria, Ghana Feed cost reduction

Source: Compiled from FAO (2019) The State of Food and Agriculture: Moving Forward on Food Loss and Waste Reduction and African Circular Economy Alliance case studies.

4. Carbon Footprint Measurement in Supply Chains

Carbon footprint measurement follows the GHG Protocol: Scope 1 (direct emissions from owned operations), Scope 2 (purchased electricity), and Scope 3 (all other indirect emissionsâfertilizer production, transport, processing, land use change). For most African agribusinesses, Scope 3 dominatesâoften 80â90% of total emissionsâdriven by fertilizer use, land use change, and logistics.

Measurement steps: (1) define boundaries and functional unit (e.g., kg COâe per tonne of green beans); (2) collect activity data (fertilizer kg, diesel litres, electricity kWh, transport tonne-km); (3) apply emission factors (IPCC, DEFRA, or country-specific); (4) verify via third party if required by buyers. Tools include the Cool Farm Tool (free, farm-level) and GHG Protocol calculators.

â  SAFETY WARNING â CARBON ACCOUNTING PITFALLS

Do not report carbon footprint figures without documenting emission factors, boundaries, and data sources. Unverified or inconsistent claims can constitute greenwashing under emerging EU and African consumer protection rules, exposing your business to fines, delisting, and reputational damage. Never use a single year's data to claim "carbon neutral"âland use change and seasonal variation require multi-year averaging.

5. Regulations and Standards for Sustainability

African agribusinesses face a layered regulatory environment: international buyer requirements, African regional frameworks, and national laws. Key instruments include:

  • EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR): Requires geolocation and due diligence for cocoa, coffee, palm oil, soy, rubber, cattle, and wood entering the EU from December 2025 (large operators).
  • EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD): Mandates human rights and environmental due diligence across value chains.
  • AfCFTA Environmental Provisions: The African Continental Free Trade Area includes sustainable development chapters encouraging green trade.
  • National laws: Kenya's Environmental Management and Co-ordination Act, Ghana's Environmental Protection Agency Act, Nigeria's NESREA regulations.
  • Voluntary standards: Rainforest Alliance, Fairtrade, Organic (EU 2018/848), GlobalG.A.P.

6. Case Study: Patagonia's Sustainable Supply Chain

Patagonia, the US outdoor clothing company, is a benchmark for supply chain sustainability. Its approach: traceable supply chains (down to raw material), the Footprint Chronicles (public disclosure of factory impacts), Fair Trade Certified sewing, and the Worn Wear repair/reuse programme. In 2022, founder Yvon Chouinard transferred ownership to a trust and non-profit dedicated to fighting climate change. For African agribusiness, the lesson is that transparency and reverse logistics (repair, reuse, take-back) build brand equity and customer loyaltyâbut they require investment in traceability systems and supplier partnerships. African parallels exist: Olam's cocoa traceability in Ghana, Sainsbury's Fairtrade tea from Kenya, and the Kering Group's sourcing from South African mohair farms.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Map your supply chain: Identify all Tier 1 and Tier 2 suppliers, their locations, and environmental risk levels.
  2. Adopt a supplier code of conduct: Include deforestation, pesticide, water, labour, and traceability clauses with audit rights.
  3. Measure your carbon footprint: Use GHG Protocol, document emission factors, and verify before making public claims.
  4. Establish reverse logistics: Set up collection systems for packaging, organic waste, and by-products with clear revenue or cost-saving targets.
  5. Track TBL metrics monthly: Financial, social, and environmental KPIs reported to management alongside financial accounts.
  6. Align with regulations: Check EUDR, CSDDD, national environmental laws, and buyer-specific standards before each export season.
  7. Train suppliers: Run farmer field schools and supplier workshops on compliance, record-keeping, and safe pesticide handling.
  8. Verify and communicate: Use third-party audits and avoid unsubstantiated green claims that risk greenwashing penalties.

Further Reading

  • FAO â The State of Food and Agriculture: Moving Forward on Food Loss and Waste Reduction (2019)
  • GHG Protocol â Corporate and Value Chain (Scope 3) Accounting Standards
  • Rainforest Alliance â 2020 Sustainable Agriculture Standard
  • European Commission â EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) Official Page
  • African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) Secretariat â Official Resources

quiz.q: What are the three Ps of the Triple Bottom Line?
quiz.explanation: The Triple Bottom Line measures success through Profit, People, and Planet.

quiz.q: Which tool can help a small African business start measuring its Triple Bottom Line?
quiz.explanation: A simple Excel scorecard with metrics for each P is a practical starting tool.

quiz.q: Why is the Triple Bottom Line important for African supply chains?
options: A) It helps attract impact investors and meet buyer demands
C) It eliminates all business risks
D) It replaces the need for profit
quiz.explanation: TBL can attract impact investors and satisfy buyers who require sustainability documentation.

quiz.q: What is green procurement?
options: B) Buying goods with least environmental impact
C) Buying from any local supplier
D) Buying only from international suppliers
quiz.explanation: Green procurement means purchasing goods and services that minimize environmental harm.

quiz.q: Which international standard is commonly requested for environmental management?
quiz.explanation: ISO 14001 is the international standard for environmental management systems.

quiz.q: What should you do if a supplier is not compliant with environmental rules?
options: B) Ignore it if they are cheap
C) Work with them on a corrective action plan
D) Report them to the police
quiz.explanation: Collaborating on a corrective action plan helps improve compliance and maintain supply.

quiz.q: What is reverse logistics?
options: A) Moving goods from producer to customer
B) Moving goods from customer back to producer
C) Storing goods in a warehouse
quiz.explanation: Reverse logistics involves the flow of goods from the end customer back to the producer for returns, repairs, or recycling.

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of circular economy?
quiz.explanation: Refilling glass bottles keeps materials in use, a key principle of circular economy.

quiz.q: How can African businesses benefit from reverse logistics?
options: A) By reducing raw material costs and creating jobs
quiz.explanation: Reverse logistics can lower costs through reuse and recycling, and create jobs in collection and processing.

quiz.q: What is a carbon footprint?
options: A) The total greenhouse gases emitted by activities
B) The weight of carbon in a product
C) The area of land used
D) The amount of water consumed
quiz.explanation: Carbon footprint measures total greenhouse gas emissions in CO2 equivalent.

quiz.q: Which scope of emissions includes purchased electricity?
quiz.explanation: Scope 2 covers indirect emissions from purchased electricity, heat, or steam.

quiz.q: What is an emission factor?
options: A) A number to multiply activity data to get emissions
quiz.explanation: Emission factors convert activity data (e.g., litres of diesel) into CO2 equivalent emissions.

quiz.q: Which action can reduce a company's carbon footprint?
options: A) Switching from air freight to sea freight
quiz.explanation: Sea freight emits far less CO2 per tonne-kilometre than air freight.

quiz.q: Why should African suppliers measure their carbon footprint?
options: A) To meet buyer requirements and save costs
quiz.explanation: Many international buyers require carbon footprint data, and measuring can identify cost-saving efficiencies.

quiz.q: What is the GHG Protocol?
options: A) A global standard for measuring greenhouse gases
B) A type of renewable energy
D) A certification for organic farming
quiz.explanation: The GHG Protocol provides standards and tools for measuring and managing greenhouse gas emissions.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sustainability regulation in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: EMCA is Kenya's Environmental Management and Co-ordination Act.

quiz.q: What does the EU's CBAM aim to do?
options: A) Tax imports based on carbon footprint
B) Ban all imports from Africa
quiz.explanation: CBAM is a carbon border adjustment mechanism that will levy charges on carbon-intensive imports.

quiz.q: Which certification is commonly required for agricultural exports?
quiz.explanation: GlobalG.A.P. is a widely recognized standard for good agricultural practices.

quiz.q: How can small African farmers afford certification?
options: C) By paying high fees individually
D) By exporting only to Africa
quiz.explanation: Group certification allows smallholders to share the cost and meet standards collectively.

quiz.q: What should a business do to prepare for a sustainability audit?
options: A) Keep records of waste disposal, training, and wages
quiz.explanation: Maintaining proper records is essential for demonstrating compliance during audits.

quiz.q: What is Patagonia's mission related to?
options: A) Building the best product and causing no unnecessary harm
B) Maximizing profit at any cost
quiz.explanation: Patagonia's mission includes building the best product, causing no unnecessary harm, and inspiring environmental solutions.

quiz.q: Which tool does Patagonia use to measure material impacts?
quiz.explanation: The Higg Index is a suite of tools for measuring environmental and social impacts of materials.

quiz.q: What is Patagonia's Worn Wear program?
options: A) A repair service for old clothes
quiz.explanation: Worn Wear repairs broken items, extending product life and reducing waste.

quiz.q: How does Patagonia practice reverse logistics?
options: A) Through take-back programs for old clothes
C) By selling only new products
quiz.explanation: Patagonia's take-back program collects old clothes for recycling into new fibers.

quiz.q: What can an African clothing brand learn from Patagonia?
options: A) Start a repair service for uniforms
quiz.explanation: A repair service extends product life and reduces waste, similar to Patagonia's Worn Wear.

quiz.q: What percentage of sales does Patagonia donate to environmental causes?
quiz.explanation: Patagonia donates 1% of sales to grassroots environmental activism.

quiz.q: Which of these is a key takeaway from Patagonia's supply chain?
options: A) Collaborate with suppliers to improve
B) Punish suppliers for any mistake
quiz.explanation: Patagonia works with suppliers to improve sustainability rather than simply dropping them.

quiz.q: What is one benefit of circular economy for African businesses?
quiz.explanation: Circular economy keeps materials in use, reducing the need for new raw materials and lowering costs.

quiz.q: Which of these is a practical step to start green procurement?
options: C) Buy from the cheapest source only
quiz.explanation: Reviewing top suppliers helps identify where to focus green procurement efforts.

quiz.q: What is the first step in measuring a carbon footprint?
options: A) Track fuel and electricity bills
quiz.explanation: Tracking fuel and electricity use provides activity data needed to calculate emissions.
